claims.text: Single-phase solid-solution formation in rapidly synthesized noble-metal HEA nanoparticles containing more than five elements is governed primarily by kinetic trapping combined with statistical dilution.
Rapid heating and ultrafast cooling severely limit atomic mobility.
Limited atomic mobility can trap atoms in a disordered, mixed state despite unfavorable element-element interactions.
Increasing the number of atom types makes random-alloy formation more likely when free-atom mobility is limited.
The low local concentration of each element statistically suppresses local ordering and elemental clustering.
Reduction of solid, mixed precursors limits free atomic mobility during noble-metal nanoparticle formation.
The initial material consists of noble-metal salt precursors deposited on a carbon-based support.
Rapid Joule heating of this precursor state produces kinetically trapped, uniformly mixed HEA nanoparticles.
Extending the dwell time at the same peak temperature increases atomic migration or diffusion.
The degree of atomic mixing and limited diffusion length determine whether atoms remain randomly dispersed or segregate into secondary phases.
A dwell-time increase from tens of milliseconds to a few seconds at approximately 1100 K will enable local segregation and phase separation.
An extended dwell will produce more elemental segregation than the rapid-synthesis baseline.
An extended dwell will produce secondary phases or intermetallic compounds relative to the single-phase baseline.
An extended dwell may produce less uniform particle morphology.
A 55 ms heating pulse followed by ultrafast cooling produces a single-phase, randomly mixed solid solution across all constituent elements.
The relevant processing regime is approximately 1100 K under inert gas with cooling rates of 10^4 to 10^5 K/s.
The proposed mechanism applies to systems containing more than five noble metals processed from solid precursors under nonequilibrium conditions.
Processing deviations that promote diffusion, including longer dwell times, will lead to phase separation.
The dwell-time threshold for segregation depends on the elemental combination and detailed processing conditions.
